title: Problem 05
markdown:
### Problem
Some positive integers have the property that if you cube the number and add up the decimal digits, you get the original number. For example, $8^3 = 512$ and $5 + 1 + 2 = 8$. Also, $17^3 = 4913$ and $4 + 9 + 1 + 3 = 17$. Are there infinitely many such integers? Defend your answer.

### Solution (adapted from the official solution)
No, there are only finitely many such integers. In fact, all of them are smaller than 100.

Suppose the positive integer $n$ has $k$ digits in base 10. Then:

$$10^{k-1} \le n < 10^k.$$

Cubing gives $n^3 < 10^{3k}$, so $n^3$ has at most $3k$ digits.
The sum of the decimal digits of $n^3$, denoted $S(n^3)$, is at most the sum of $3k$ nines:

$$S(n^3) \le 9(3k) = 27k.$$

If $27k < 10^{k-1}$, then $S(n^3) \le 27k < 10^{k-1} \le n$, making $S(n^3) = n$ impossible.

We show by induction that $27k < 10^{k-1}$ for all $k \ge 3$:
- For $k = 3$: $27(3) = 81 < 10^2 = 100$.
- For $k \ge 3$, assume $27k < 10^{k-1}$. Then:
$$27(k+1) = 27k + 27 < 10^{k-1} + 10^2 \le 2 \times 10^{k-1} < 10 \times 10^{k-1} = 10^k.$$

Thus by induction, $27k < 10^{k-1}$ holds for all $k \ge 3$. Therefore no integer with 3 or more digits can satisfy $S(n^3) = n$, bounding all solutions below 100.

### Conceptual Explanation
A $k$-digit number $n \ge 10^{k-1}$ has a cube with at most $3k$ digits, so the digit sum is at most $27k$. Because exponential growth $10^{k-1}$ rapidly outpaces linear growth $27k$ for all $k \ge 3$, only numbers with $k \le 2$ (i.e. $n < 100$) can satisfy the condition.

### Key Technique
Bounding digit sums $S(n^3) \le 27k$ against exponential lower bounds $n \ge 10^{k-1}$.
